t: Count Numbers With Unique Digits II
o: We must count integers in [a, b] (with b ≤ 1000) whose decimal digits are all distinct. In Example 1, [1,20] loses only 11, giving 19. In Example 3, [80,120] keeps 27 of 41 numbers (e.g. 100, 101, 110 are rejected). Since b ≤ 1000, the range has at most 1000 numbers, so even inspecting every number is trivially fast; the constraints mean no fancy math is required, though a digit-DP-style incremental computation is a nice pattern to practice for the general version of this problem.
k: With b ≤ 1000, brute-force checking every number in [a, b] is at most 1000 cheap checks.
A number has unique digits iff its last digit does not appear in its prefix — this enables an incremental DP over 1..b.

a.i: For each number in [a, b], convert it to a string (or extract digits arithmetically) and test whether all digits are distinct by comparing set size to length. This directly mirrors the definition and is instantaneous for the given bounds.
s: Iterate x from a to b.
Convert x to a string; it is valid if len(set(str(x))) == len(str(x)).
Return the count of valid x.
a.t: O((b − a + 1) · d) where d ≤ 4 digits — we scan the whole range once.
a.sp: O(d) for the temporary digit representation.

a.i: Define good[x] = 'x has unique digits'. Then good[x] holds iff good[x // 10] holds and the last digit of x does not appear in x // 10. Tracking a 10-bit mask of digits seen in the prefix lets us compute validity for every number up to b in O(1) amortized, then answer with a prefix count over [a, b]. This scales gracefully if bounds grow.
s: Compute mask[x] = mask[x // 10] | bit(last digit) and good[x] = good[x // 10] and bit not already set, for x = 1..b.
Accumulate a running count of good numbers.
a.t: O(b) — one pass computing validity for every number up to b.

w: In an interview, lead with the brute force since bounds make it optimal in practice, then offer the incremental-DP version to show you can generalize to large bounds (where a proper digit DP counting numbers ≤ n with distinct digits would be the real answer). Pitfall: remember single-digit numbers are always valid, and the range is inclusive on both ends. A likely follow-up is the classic 'Count Numbers with Unique Digits' for arbitrary digit lengths, solved with permutations 9·9·8·…
